prompt.brief: Design a governed data lake that ingests batch and streaming sources, preserves raw structured/unstructured data, catalogs schemas and lineage, enables performant SQL, and serves trusted analytics.
successSignals: Define raw, validated, curated, and aggregate zones; dataset ownership, schema contracts, partitions, retention, lineage, and quality gates.
Separate ingestion from compaction, cataloging, transformation, query engines, and BI serving; optimize file sizes and partition pruning.
Handle late data, schema evolution, duplicates, backfills, sensitive fields, deletion requests, and exactly-once or replay semantics.
Explain governance, cost controls, isolation, query correctness, disaster recovery, observability, and degraded query behavior.

functional: Ingest files, database changes, and streams into durable raw zones; validate, deduplicate, transform, catalog, and publish curated tables.
Provide dataset discovery, schema/lineage views, SQL queries, materialized aggregates, BI access, freshness and quality status.
Support role/row/column access, retention/deletion, replay/backfill, schema approval, failed-batch quarantine, and restore testing.
nonFunctional: Return common partition-pruned analytical queries with p95 under 10 seconds and publish freshness/quality metadata.
Scale to petabytes and thousands of concurrent workloads without a single hot key or unbounded synchronous work.
Do not lose committed state; make retries and duplicate events safe.
Degrade safely when downstream workers, caches, or external dependencies fail.
scaleAssumptions: 5PB retained, 100TB daily ingest, and 10k concurrent analytical users
Partition by the primary tenant, user, item, or geographic key and isolate hot partitions.
Keep serving state bounded; retain raw events or durable records for replay and auditing.

architecture.title: Scalable Data Lake Architecture data platform architecture
architecture.summary: Design a governed data lake that ingests batch and streaming sources, preserves raw structured/unstructured data, catalogs schemas and lineage, enables performant SQL, and serves trusted analytics. The design preserves immutable source evidence and contracts, processes partitions with checkpointed batch or streaming jobs, and serves curated results with freshness and quality metadata.

deepDives.title: Schema evolution and data quality
points: Version scalable data lake architecture contracts and make compatibility rules explicit for every producer and consumer.
Quarantine malformed partitions instead of poisoning the whole dataset.
Track row counts, null rates, duplicates, distribution changes, and policy violations by partition.

deepDives.title: Watermarks, late data, and exactly-once effects
points: Use source cursors and event-time watermarks for scalable data lake architecture progress, not wall-clock assumptions.
Make checkpoints, output keys, and sink commits retry-safe under at-least-once delivery.
Document how late events revise windows, aggregates, or snapshots.

deepDives.title: Replay, lineage, and cost
points: Keep immutable scalable data lake architecture raw evidence and code or schema versions so failed outputs can be reproduced.
Separate hot serving storage from cold retention and cap replay concurrency.
Measure freshness, backlog, compute cost, storage growth, and quality-gate failure rate.

tradeoffs.title: Streaming versus batch
tradeoffs.recommendation: Use streaming for freshness-critical scalable data lake architecture paths and batch for backfills, compaction, and expensive recomputation.
tradeoffs.caution: Forcing every workload into streaming makes state, replay, and cost harder to operate.

tradeoffs.title: Raw retention versus curated-only storage
tradeoffs.recommendation: Retain enough immutable raw evidence for replay, audit, and correction, then tier or expire it according to policy.
tradeoffs.caution: Without raw evidence, a bad transformation can require an unreproducible emergency fix.

tradeoffs.title: Central warehouse versus domain-owned datasets
tradeoffs.recommendation: Centralize governance and discovery while letting domain owners own contracts and quality signals.
tradeoffs.caution: A single team owning every transformation becomes a delivery bottleneck and hides data ownership.

commonMistakes: Treating scalable data lake architecture ingestion success as proof that downstream data is complete or correct.
Dropping late events or schema failures without a quarantine and replay path.
Using wall-clock processing time where event-time windows and watermarks are required.
Overwriting curated data in place without run, code, schema, or input lineage.
Ignoring backlog, freshness, quality, storage, and compute-cost signals until consumers report stale data.

followUps.question: How do you replay a failed scalable data lake architecture partition?
followUps.answer: Retain source cursor and watermark, rerun a versioned transformation into an isolated output, validate quality, then atomically publish the replacement.

followUps.question: How do you handle schema changes?
followUps.answer: Register a new version, validate compatibility, dual-read or dual-write when needed, and expose the active contract to consumers.

followUps.question: What does exactly once mean here?
followUps.answer: It means the combination of durable checkpoints, deterministic output identities, and idempotent sinks prevents duplicate business effects; transport alone remains at least once.

rubric.description: The answer addresses the scalable data lake architecture workflow, scale, latency, durability, authorization, and failure contract.
The answer identifies the authoritative scalable data lake architecture state, versioning or deduplication boundary, and how derived views converge.
The answer partitions scalable data lake architecture traffic, isolates hot keys, and moves fan-out, retries, or rebuilds behind bounded asynchronous work.
The answer names freshness, backlog, error, cost, and recovery signals tied to the scalable data lake architecture user experience.
